Your write-up correctly recalls the defining equation  
  x + 0 = x  
but at the moment it stops short of turning that fact into a genuine proof that “if x + y = x then y = 0.” In particular, you have not shown why no other y can satisfy x + y = x except y = 0. Here are a few suggestions on how to fill in the missing steps:

    “Assume x + y = x.  I want to deduce y = 0.”

2.  Notice that by the definition of addition, for every y there is a (unique) element x + y.  You used “uniqueness” informally, but we need a precise reason: injectivity of certain maps coming from the Peano axioms.

3.  A standard approach is by induction on y:

    •  Base case y=0: then x + 0=x, so x + y=x holds. In the reverse direction, if x + y=x and you already know x+0=x, you see y=0 is a valid candidate.  

    •  Inductive step: assume for some n that “if x + y=x then y=0” holds for y=n. Now consider y=ν(n). If x + ν(n)=x, then by definition x + ν(n)=ν(x+n). So ν(x+n)=x. But no natural number maps under ν to 0 (Peano axiom P3), so x cannot equal ν(…) unless we also know x itself has the form ν(m). More systematically, one shows that ν is injective (P4), so from
       ν(x+n)=ν(0) 
    you get x+n=0, which is absurd because 0 has no predecessor.  A cleaner version is: compare x + ν(n) with x + 0, get ν(x+n)=ν(0), then apply injectivity of ν to conclude x+n=0. 4.  Alternatively, one can first prove the general Cancellation Law: if x + a = x + b then a=b, by induction on x or on one of the summands.  Once you have that, your proof is just two lines:
     
     •  x + y = x + 0  
     •  by cancellation, y = 0.  

Either route—direct induction on y or a cancellation theorem—gives a complete proof that y must be zero.  

What you’ve written already shows you know the key defining fact x + 0 = x, which is good. Next time, be sure to:

•  State the assumption and goal clearly.  
•  Invoke the appropriate Peano axiom (injectivity of the successor map or the cancellation law you proved earlier).  
•  Flesh out the induction or cancellation argument to close the logical gap.

What you did well  
1. You zeroed in on the key observation: whenever one of the summands is a successor, the sum is also a successor, so by Peano axiom P3 it cannot equal 0.  
2. You invoked the recursive definition of addition, \(x + \nu(y)=\nu(x+y)\), to see immediately that \(x+\nu(y)\) can never be 0.

1. Lack of structure.  A clear “case‐analysis” format would make your argument easier to follow.  In particular, you want to argue:  
   – Case A: \(y\) is a successor, say \(y=\nu(y')\).  Then \(x+y = x+\nu(y') = \nu(x+y')\).  By P3 no successor can be 0, so this case contradicts the assumption \(x+y=0\).  
   – Case B: \(y=0\).  Then \(x+y = x+0 = x\).  From \(x+y=0\) we get \(x=0\).  

2. Missing the use of commutativity.  You only treated the case in which the second summand is a successor.  If you want to avoid a separate “\(x\) is successor” case, you should explicitly invoke commutativity of addition:  
   \[
     x + y = y + x,
   \]  
   so when you find that \(y\neq 0\) leads to a contradiction, you don’t need to run through the same argument again swapping the roles of \(x\) and \(y\).  

3. Explicitly cite the axioms you use.  You appealed to P3 in words but did not tag it in your write-up.  And when you conclude \(x+0=x\), that is exactly the defining axiom of addition.  If you ever need to invoke injectivity (P4) or induction later, it’s helpful practice to label each step with the axiom or definition you’re using.

A polished version might look like this:

Proof.  Suppose \(x+y=0\).  We proceed by cases on \(y\).

Case 1: \(y=\nu(y')\) for some \(y'\).  Then by the recursive definition of addition,
\[
  x+y \;=\; x+\nu(y') \;=\; \nu\bigl(x+y'\bigr).
\]
But \(\nu\bigl(x+y'\bigr)\) is a successor, and by P3 no successor equals 0.  Hence this case contradicts \(x+y=0\).

Case 2: \(y=0\).  Then
\[
  x+y \;=\; x+0 \;=\; x
\]
by definition of addition.  Since \(x+y=0\), we obtain \(x=0\).

Therefore the only possibility is \(x=0\) and \(y=0\), as required.  Notice that by commutativity one does not need to repeat the successor‐case argument with \(x\) in the second slot.

This proof clearly indicates (i) the case distinction, (ii) each axiom or definition used, and (iii) the role of commutativity in collapsing the two “successor‐cases” into one.

   P(λ) = (u + λv)·(u + λv)  
and using the fact that P(λ) ≥ 0 for all real λ to force the discriminant to be non‐positive.  From that you extract  
   (u·v)² ≤ (u·u)(v·v),  
which is exactly the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.  This is precisely the approach we discussed in class, so you’re on the right track.  

Here are a few suggestions to tighten up the presentation and clear up small errors:

1.  **Write out P(λ) carefully.**  
    Your expansion should read  
       P(λ) = u·u  +  2λ (u·v)  +  λ² (v·v).  
    In your write‐up the middle term lost its factor of λ.  

2.  **Explain the link to the discriminant.**  
    You wrote “it can have at most one (repeated) real solution, due to inner products yielding results ≥0.”  A clearer way is:  
    – Since P(λ) ≥ 0 for every real λ, the quadratic cannot change sign, so it cannot have two distinct real roots.  
    – Equivalently, the discriminant Δ = [2(u·v)]² − 4(u·u)(v·v) must satisfy Δ ≤ 0.  

3.  **Be precise about absolute values.**  
    After you derive (u·v)² ≤ (u·u)(v·v), you can immediately take square roots to get  
       |u·v| ≤ √(u·u) √(v·v) = |u| |v|.  

4.  **Equality‐case computations.**  
    – If u = k v then u·v = k (v·v), so |u·v| = |k| |v|², while |u||v| = |k||v|² as well.

5.  **Minor remark on the zero‐vector case.**

     area D(R−√2) ≤ ∑ area S(m,n) = f(R)·1 = f(R).  
   •  Hence π(R−√2)² ≤ f(R).

Here is some detailed feedback on your write‐up:

1. Overall structure and ideas  
   • You correctly recognized that one must work in polar coordinates and decompose the dog’s velocity into a radial part and an orthoradial (tangential) part.  
   • You set up a first–order differential equation for r versus θ, which is exactly the right approach to find the curve.  

2. The key kinematic slip  
   In polar coordinates the dog’s instantaneous velocity components are  
     – radial:      v_r = dr/dt  = –v cos(π/N)  
     – tangential: v_θ = r (dθ/dt) =  v sin(π/N)  
   (because the dog always runs directly along the chord to its neighbour, which makes an angle π/N with the radial direction.)  
   
   In your solution you wrote simply  
     dθ/dt = v cos(π/N),

     r (dθ/dt) = v sin(π/N).

     dr/dt   = –v cos(π/N),  
     dθ/dt  =  [v sin(π/N)] / r,
